fields.title: The Life of Blaise Pascal
fields.subtitle: By Madame Périer, His Sister
fields.description: Gilberte Périer, Pascal's elder sister, wrote this life soon after his death. She tells of the boy who worked out Euclid's geometry for himself, the inventor of the calculating machine, the family's conversion at Rouen and her brother's withdrawal from the world; then she lingers over his love of poverty, his charity to the poor, his patience in sickness, and the last days when he asked that a poor sick man be brought into the house to die in his company.
fields.attribution: AI translation, awaiting review, of Gilberte Périer's Vie de Blaise Pascal (published 1684), made from the French text of the Œuvres complètes de Blaise Pascal (Hachette, 1871) on Wikisource. The French original is in the library; the four parts are the Ochorus editor's.

fields.title: His Childhood and Early Work
fields.body_html:
My brother was born at Clermont on the 19th of June in the year 1623. My father's name was Étienne Pascal, president of the Cour des Aides; and my mother's, Antoinette Begon. As soon as my brother was old enough to be talked to, he gave signs of an extraordinary mind by the little retorts he made, very much to the point, but still more by the questions he asked about the nature of things, which surprised everyone. This beginning, which gave such fair hopes, never belied itself; for as he grew he kept increasing in strength of reasoning, so that he was always far beyond his age.

Meanwhile, my mother having died as early as the year 1626, when my brother was only three years old, my father, finding himself alone, applied himself more earnestly to the care of his family; and as he had no other son but this one, his being an only son, together with the great signs of intelligence he recognised in the child, gave him so great an affection for him that he could not bring himself to entrust his education to another, and resolved from that time to teach him himself, as indeed he did, my brother never having entered any college, and never having had any other master than my father.

In the year 1631 my father withdrew to Paris, took us all there, and made his home there. My brother, who was only eight years old, gained a great advantage from this retirement, in view of my father's plan for his upbringing; for there is no doubt that he could not have taken the same care in the provinces, where the duties of his office and the continual company that came to his house would have greatly distracted him; but in Paris he was entirely free; he gave himself wholly to it, and he had all the success that could come of the care of a father as intelligent and as affectionate as a father can be.

His chief maxim in this education was always to keep the child above his work; and it was for this reason that he would not begin to teach him Latin until he was twelve, so that he might learn it with greater ease.

During this interval he did not leave him idle, for he talked with him about everything he saw him capable of understanding. He showed him in a general way what languages were; he showed him how they had been reduced to grammars under certain rules; that these rules had in turn exceptions which people had taken care to note; and that in this way a means had been found of making every language communicable from one country to another.

This general idea cleared his mind and showed him the reason for the rules of grammar, so that when he came to learn it he knew why he was doing so, and he applied himself precisely to the things that most required application.

After this knowledge my father gave him other kinds; he often spoke to him of the extraordinary effects of nature, such as gunpowder, and other things that astonish us when we consider them. My brother took great pleasure in these conversations, but he wanted to know the reason for everything; and since the reasons are not all known, when my father did not give them, or gave those commonly put forward, which are really nothing but evasions, he was not satisfied: for he always had an admirable clearness of mind for discerning what is false; and one may say that always and in all things truth was the sole object of his mind, since nothing could ever satisfy him but the knowledge of it. Thus from his childhood he could yield only to what appeared to him evidently true; so that when he was not given good reasons he looked for them himself, and when he had fastened on something he would not let it go until he had found some reason that could satisfy him. Once, among other occasions, someone at table having struck an earthenware dish with a knife, he noticed that it gave out a loud sound, but that as soon as a hand was laid on it the sound stopped. He wished at once to know the cause, and this experiment led him to make many others on sounds. He observed so many things that he wrote a treatise on them at the age of twelve, which was judged to be altogether well reasoned.

His genius for geometry began to appear when he was still only twelve, through so extraordinary an occurrence that it seems to me well worth relating in detail.

My father was a man learned in mathematics, and through this was acquainted with all the able men in that science, who were often at his house; but since he intended to instruct my brother in languages, and knew that mathematics is a science that fills and greatly satisfies the mind, he did not wish my brother to have any knowledge of it, for fear it should make him neglectful of Latin and the other [sciences] in which he wished to perfect him. For this reason he had put away all the books that dealt with it, and he refrained from speaking of it with his friends in his presence; but this precaution did not prevent the child's curiosity from being aroused, so that he often begged my father to teach him mathematics; but my father refused, holding it out to him as a reward. He promised him that as soon as he knew Latin and Greek he would teach it to him. My brother, seeing this resistance, asked him one day what this science was and what it dealt with: my father told him, in general terms, that it was the means of making figures correctly and of finding the proportions they bore to one another, and at the same time forbade him to speak of it any more or ever to think of it. But this mind, which could not stay within such bounds, no sooner had this simple opening—that mathematics gave the means of making figures that were unfailingly correct—than he began to muse on it by himself in his hours of recreation; and being alone in a room where he was accustomed to play, he would take a piece of charcoal and draw figures on the floor tiles, seeking ways to make, for example, a perfectly round circle, a triangle whose sides and angles were all equal, and other such things. He found all this out by himself; then he sought the proportions of the figures to one another. But as my father had taken such great care to hide all these things from him, he did not even know their names. He was obliged to make up definitions for himself; he called a circle a “round,” a line a “bar,” and so with the rest. After these definitions he made himself axioms, and finally he made perfect demonstrations; and as in these matters one proceeds from one thing to the next, he pushed his inquiries so far that he reached the thirty-second proposition of the first book of Euclid. While he was at this point, my father came into the room where he was, without my brother hearing him; he found him so intently absorbed that it was a long while before he noticed his coming. One cannot say which of them was the more surprised: the son to see his father, because of the express prohibition he had been given, or the father to see his son in the midst of all these things. But the father's surprise was far greater when, having asked him what he was doing, he was told that he was looking for such-and-such a thing, which was the thirty-second proposition of the first book of Euclid. My father asked him what had made him think of looking for that: he said it was because he had found such-and-such another thing; and when my father put the same question to him again, he told him of some further demonstrations he had made; and at last, working backwards and always explaining himself by the names “round” and “bar,” he came to his definitions and his axioms.

My father was so overwhelmed by the greatness and power of this genius that, without saying a word to him, he left him and went to the house of M. Le Pailleur, who was his intimate friend and also a very learned man. When he arrived there he stood motionless, like a man beside himself. M. Le Pailleur, seeing this, and seeing too that he was shedding some tears, was alarmed, and begged him not to hide from him any longer the cause of his distress. My father answered him: “I am not weeping for sorrow, but for joy. You know the pains I have taken to keep the knowledge of geometry from my son, for fear of turning him from his other studies: and yet see what he has done.” Upon this he showed him everything the boy had found, from which one might say that in a manner he had invented mathematics. M. Le Pailleur was no less surprised than my father had been, and told him that he did not think it right to hold this mind captive any longer and to keep this knowledge from it still; that he ought to let him see the books, without restraining him further.

My father, thinking this advisable, gave him Euclid's Elements to read in his hours of recreation. He went through them and understood them entirely by himself, without ever needing any explanation; and while he was going through them he was composing, and advanced so far that he regularly attended the meetings held every week, where all the able men of Paris gathered to bring their own works or to examine those of others. My brother held his own there very well, both in examining and in producing; for he was among those who most often brought new things. There were also often seen at these gatherings propositions sent from Italy, Germany and other foreign countries, and his opinion was sought on everything with as much care as that of any of the others; for his insight was so keen that it sometimes happened that he discovered errors which the others had not noticed. Yet he gave to this study of geometry only his hours of recreation; for he was learning Latin by rules my father had drawn up expressly for him. But as he found in this science the truth he had so ardently sought, he was so satisfied with it that he put his whole mind into it; so that, however little he applied himself, he advanced so far that at the age of sixteen he wrote a treatise on Conics which was held to be so great a feat of intellect that it was said nothing of such power had been seen since Archimedes. The learned were of the opinion that it should be printed at once, for they said that, although it was a work that would always be admirable, yet if it were printed at a time when its inventor was still only sixteen, that circumstance would add much to its beauty: but as my brother never had any passion for reputation, he made no account of this; and so the work has never been printed.

Throughout all this time he went on learning Latin and Greek; and besides this, during and after meals my father would talk with him now of logic, now of physics and the other parts of philosophy; and that is all he ever learned of them, having never been to college, nor had any other masters for these subjects any more than for the rest. My father took such pleasure as may be imagined in the great progress my brother was making in all the sciences, but he did not notice that such great and continual application at so tender an age might seriously affect his health; and in fact it began to be impaired as soon as he reached the age of eighteen. But as the ailments he then felt were not yet very severe, they did not prevent him from continuing his usual occupations; so that it was at that time, at the age of eighteen, that he invented the arithmetical machine by which one can perform not only every kind of calculation without pen or counters, but can even do so without knowing any rule of arithmetic, and with unfailing accuracy.

This work was regarded as something new in nature: to have reduced to a machine a science that resides wholly in the mind, and to have found the means of performing all its operations with complete certainty, without any need of reasoning. This labour tired him greatly, not on account of the idea or the mechanism, which he found without difficulty, but in making the workmen understand all these things. So that he spent two years bringing it to the perfection in which it now stands.

But this fatigue, and the delicate state his health had been in for some years, brought on ailments that never afterwards left him; so that he would sometimes tell us that since the age of eighteen he had not passed a day without pain. Yet as these ailments were not always equally violent, as soon as he had a little rest and respite his mind would turn at once to seeking something new.

It was at that time, at the age of twenty-three, that, having seen Torricelli's experiment, he went on to devise and carry out the other experiments that are called his experiments: those on the vacuum, which proved so clearly that all the effects hitherto attributed to nature's abhorrence of a vacuum are caused by the weight of the air. This was the last occupation in which he applied his mind to the human sciences; and although he discovered the cycloid afterwards, that does not contradict what I say; for he found it without thinking of it, and in a way that shows plainly he gave it no application, as I shall tell in its place.

fields.title: His Conversion and Retreat
fields.body_html:
Immediately after this experiment, and when he was not yet twenty-four years old, Providence having brought about an occasion that led him to read works of piety, God so enlightened him through this reading that he understood perfectly that the Christian religion obliges us to live for God alone and to have no other object but him; and this truth appeared to him so evident, so necessary and so profitable that it put an end to all his researches: so that from that time he renounced every other kind of knowledge, to apply himself solely to the one thing that Jesus Christ calls needful.

Until then he had been preserved, by a particular protection of God, from all the vices of youth; and, what is stranger still in a mind of that temper and character, he had never inclined to free-thinking in matters of religion, having always confined his curiosity to natural things. He told me several times that he added this obligation to all the others he owed to my father, who, having himself a very great respect for religion, had instilled it in him from childhood, giving him as a maxim that whatever is the object of faith cannot be the object of reason, and much less be subject to it. These maxims, often repeated to him by a father for whom he had a very great esteem, and in whom he saw great learning joined with very clear and powerful reasoning, made so great an impression on his mind that, whatever talk he heard from the free-thinkers, he was not in the least moved by it; and young as he was, he regarded them as people who held the false principle that human reason is above all things, and who did not know the nature of faith; and so this mind, so great, so vast and so full of curiosity, which sought with such care the cause and reason of everything, was at the same time as submissive as a child to all the things of religion; and this simplicity reigned in him all his life: so that, even after he resolved to make no other study than that of religion, he never applied himself to the curious questions of theology, but put all the strength of his mind into knowing and practising the perfection of Christian morals, to which he consecrated all the talents God had given him, doing nothing else for the whole rest of his life but meditate on the law of God day and night. But although he had made no special study of scholastic theology, he was not ignorant of the Church's decisions against the heresies that have been devised by subtlety of mind; and it was against inquiries of that kind that he was most roused, and God gave him from that time an occasion to show the zeal he had for religion.

He was then at Rouen, where my father was employed in the King's service, and there was at that same time a man there who was teaching a new philosophy that drew all the curious. My brother, having been urged to go by two young men who were his friends, went with them: but they were much surprised, in the conversation they had with this man, to find that in setting out the principles of his philosophy he drew from them conclusions on points of faith contrary to the decisions of the Church. He argued that the body of Jesus Christ was not formed of the blood of the Holy Virgin, but of another matter created for the purpose, and several other such things. They tried to contradict him, but he remained firm in this opinion. So, having considered among themselves the danger of leaving the freedom to instruct the young to a man who held erroneous opinions, they resolved first to warn him, and then to denounce him if he resisted the warning. And so it happened, for he scorned the warning: so that they believed it their duty to denounce him to M. du Bellay, who was at that time performing the episcopal functions in the diocese of Rouen by commission of the Archbishop. M. du Bellay sent for the man and, having questioned him, was deceived by an equivocal confession of faith which the man wrote out and signed with his own hand, M. du Bellay moreover making little of a warning of such importance given him by three young men.

However, as soon as they saw this confession of faith they recognised its defect; which obliged them to go and find the Archbishop of Rouen at Gaillon, who, having examined the whole matter, found it so serious that he wrote letters patent to his council and gave M. du Bellay an express order to make the man retract on all the points of which he was accused, and to receive nothing from him except through those who had denounced him. This was carried out accordingly: he appeared before the Archbishop's council and renounced all his opinions; and one may say that he did so sincerely, for he never showed any bitterness against those who had brought this affair upon him: which leads one to believe that he himself had been deceived by the false conclusions he drew from his false principles. Indeed it was quite certain that no one had had any design in this of harming him, nor any other aim than to undeceive him in his own eyes and to prevent him from leading astray young people who would not have been able to distinguish the true from the false in such subtle questions. Thus the affair ended quietly; and as my brother went on seeking more and more the means of pleasing God, this love of Christian perfection was so kindled in him from the age of twenty-four that it spread through the whole household. My father himself, not ashamed to yield to his son's teaching, adopted from then on a stricter way of life, in the constant practice of the virtues, until his death, which was altogether Christian; and my sister, who had quite extraordinary gifts of mind, and who from her childhood had enjoyed a reputation that few girls attain, was so touched by my brother's words that she resolved to renounce all the advantages she had until then so loved, in order to consecrate herself wholly to God, as she has since done, having become a nun in a very holy and very austere house, where she made such good use of the perfections with which God had adorned her that she was found worthy of the most difficult charges, which she always fulfilled with all the faithfulness imaginable, and where she died a holy death on the 4th of October 1661, aged thirty-six.

Meanwhile my brother, whom God was using to work all this good, was afflicted by continual illnesses which kept on increasing. But as he then knew no other science than perfection, he found a great difference between it and the one that had occupied his mind until then; for whereas his infirmities had held back his progress in the others, this one, on the contrary, perfected him in those very infirmities through the admirable patience with which he bore them. To show this I shall content myself with relating one example.

Among other ailments, he could not swallow anything liquid unless it was warm, and even then he could do so only drop by drop: but as he had besides an unbearable headache, an excessive burning in his bowels and many other ills, the doctors ordered him to take a purge every other day for three months; so that all these medicines had to be taken, and for that they had to be warmed and swallowed drop by drop: which was a veritable torture, sickening to all who were near him, yet he never once complained of it.

Continuing these remedies, together with others that he was made to follow, brought him some relief, but not perfect health; so that the doctors believed that to recover entirely he must give up every kind of mental application and seek as much as he could occasions for diversion. My brother was reluctant to accept this advice, because he saw danger in it: but at last he followed it, believing himself obliged to do all he could to restore his health, and he supposed that respectable diversions could do him no harm; and so he went into society. But although, by the mercy of God, he always kept himself free from vice, nevertheless, as God was calling him to a great perfection, he would not leave him there, and he made use of my sister for this purpose, as he had once made use of my brother when he wished to draw my sister away from the ties that held her in the world.

She was then a nun, and was leading so holy a life that she edified the whole house: being in that state, it grieved her to see that the one to whom she owed, after God, the graces she enjoyed was not himself in possession of those graces; and as my brother saw her often, she often spoke to him of it too; and at last she did so with such strength and gentleness that she persuaded him of what he had been the first to persuade her—to leave the world absolutely; so that he resolved to give up altogether the society of the world and to cut away all the useless things of life, even at the risk of his health, because he believed that salvation was to be preferred to all things.

He was then thirty years old, and still in poor health; and it was from that time that he took up the manner of life in which he continued until his death.

To carry out this purpose and break all his habits, he changed his quarter of the city and went to live for some time in the country; and on his return from there he showed so plainly that he meant to leave the world that at last the world left him; and he founded the rule of his life in this retirement on two chief maxims, which were to renounce all pleasure and all superfluity; and it was in this practice that he spent the rest of his life. To succeed in it, he began from then on, as he always did afterwards, to do without the service of his servants as far as he could. He made his own bed, he went to fetch his dinner from the kitchen and carried it to his room, and he took the dishes back; in short, he made use of his household only to do his cooking, to run errands in town, and for the other things he absolutely could not do himself. All his time was spent in prayer and in reading Holy Scripture, and he took an incredible delight in it. On such occasions he would take an iron belt full of points and put it on next to his bare flesh; and whenever some thought of vanity came to him, or he took some pleasure in the place where he was, or something of the kind, he would strike it with his elbow to redouble the sharpness of the pricks, and so make himself remember his duty. This practice seemed to him so useful that he kept it up until his death, and even in the last period of his life, when he was in continual pain, because he could neither write nor read: he was forced to remain doing nothing and to go out walking. That is how he spent five years of his life, from the age of thirty to thirty-five: working without ceasing for God, for his neighbour and for himself, striving to perfect himself more and more; and one might say in a manner that this is the whole time he lived: for the four years that God gave him afterwards were nothing but a continual languishing. It was not properly an illness that had newly come upon him, but a redoubling of the grave infirmities to which he had been subject since his youth. But he was then attacked by them with such violence that at last he succumbed to them; and during all that time he was not able to work for a single moment at the great work he had undertaken for religion, nor to help the people who came to him for advice, either by word of mouth or in writing: for his sufferings were so great that he could not satisfy them, although he greatly desired to.

fields.title: His Sufferings and His Virtues
fields.body_html:
This return of his ailments began with a toothache that took away his sleep entirely. During his long wakeful hours, one night, without any intention on his part, some thoughts came into his mind concerning the problem of the cycloid (the roulette). That thought was followed by another, and that one by another, until at last a multitude of thoughts, succeeding one another, revealed to him almost in spite of himself the demonstration of all these things, at which he himself was surprised. But as he had long since renounced all such knowledge, it did not even occur to him to write it down. Nevertheless, having happened to mention it to a person to whom he owed every kind of deference, both out of respect and out of gratitude for the affection with which that person honoured him, this person—who is as distinguished for piety as for eminent qualities of mind and greatness of birth—conceived on this a plan that looked only to the glory of God, and thought it fitting that he should make use of it as he did, and afterwards have it printed. Only then did he write it out, and with extreme haste, in eight days; for it was while the printers were at work, and he was supplying two of them at once with two different treatises, without ever having any other copy than the one made for the press; and this was not known until six months later, when the matter was discovered.

Meanwhile his infirmities, continuing without giving him a single moment's respite, reduced him, as I have said, to being unable to work any longer and to seeing almost no one. But if they prevented him from serving the public and private persons, they were by no means useless to himself, and he bore them with such peace and such patience that there is reason to believe God meant by them to complete the work of making him such as He wished him to be in order to appear before Him. For during this long illness he never turned aside from these aims, keeping always in mind those two great maxims, to renounce all pleasure and all superfluity. He practised them in the very worst of his sickness, with a continual watch over his senses, absolutely refusing them everything that was agreeable to them; and when necessity forced him to do something that might give him some satisfaction, he had a wonderful skill in turning his mind away from it, so that it should take no part in it. For example, as his constant illnesses obliged him to eat delicate food, he took very great care not to taste what he ate; and we noticed that, however much trouble we took to find him some pleasant dish, because of the distaste for food to which he was subject, he never once said, “That is good”; and again, when he was served something new in its season, if he was asked after the meal whether he had enjoyed it, he would say simply, “You should have told me beforehand, for I confess I did not notice it.” And when it happened that someone in his presence admired the excellence of some dish, he could not bear it; he called that being sensual, even if it was only ordinary food, because, he said, it was a sign that one ate to please the palate, which was always wrong.

To avoid falling into this, he would never allow any sauce or ragout to be made for him, not even orange or verjuice, nor anything at all that stimulates the appetite, although by nature he was fond of all these things. And to keep himself within fixed limits, he had observed from the beginning of his retirement what his stomach required; and from then on he had settled everything he was to eat, so that, however great his appetite, he never went beyond it, and however great his distaste, he made himself eat it. And when he was asked why he constrained himself in this way, he said that it was the need of the stomach that must be satisfied, and not the appetite. The mortification of his senses went not only so far as to cut off from them everything that might be agreeable to them, but also to refuse them nothing on the ground that it might be disagreeable to them, whether in his food or in his remedies. For four years together he took broths without showing the least distaste; he took all the things prescribed for his health without any difficulty, however hard they might be; and when I was astonished that he showed not the slightest reluctance in taking them, he laughed at me and told me that he could not himself understand how anyone could show reluctance in taking a medicine voluntarily, after being warned that it was unpleasant, and that only force or surprise ought to produce that effect. It was in this way that he laboured unceasingly at mortification.

He had so great a love for poverty that it was always present to him; so that as soon as he wished to undertake anything, or someone asked his advice, the first thought that came to his mind was to see whether poverty could be practised in it. One of the things on which he examined himself most was that fancy of wishing to excel in everything, such as employing the best workmen for everything, and other things of the kind. Nor could he bear that people should carefully seek out every convenience, such as having everything close at hand, and a thousand other things that people do without scruple because they do not think there is any harm in them. But he did not judge so, and told us that there was nothing so apt to extinguish the spirit of poverty as this studied pursuit of one's comforts, and of that seemliness which makes one always want to have the best and the best made; and he told us that as for workmen, one should always choose the poorest and the most upright, and not that excellence which is never necessary and can never be of use. He would sometimes exclaim, “If my heart were as poor as my mind, I should be very happy; for I am wonderfully persuaded that poverty is a great means of working out one's salvation.”

This love he had for poverty led him to love the poor with such tenderness that he never refused alms, even though he gave only out of what he himself needed, having little property and being obliged, because of his infirmities, to incur expenses that exceeded his income. But when anyone tried to point this out to him as he was giving some considerable alms, he grew vexed and said, “I have noticed one thing: however poor one may be, one always leaves something behind at death.” Thus he closed their mouths; and he sometimes went so far that he was reduced to borrowing money at interest, having given to the poor all he had and not wishing after that to trouble his friends. As soon as the business of the coaches was established, he told me that he meant to ask a thousand francs in advance on his share from the contractors with whom terms were being negotiated, if agreement could be reached with them, since they were acquaintances of his, in order to send it to the poor of Blois; and when I told him that the business was not yet secure enough for that, and that he should wait for another year, he at once gave me this answer: that he saw no great difficulty in it, because if they lost, he would repay them out of his own property, and that he would take good care not to wait for another year, because the need was too pressing to put off charity. And as no agreement was reached with these persons, he could not carry out this resolution, by which he showed us the truth of what he had so often told us, that he wished to have wealth only in order to help the poor with it; since at the very moment when God gave him the hope of having some, he began to distribute it in advance, before he was even sure of it.

His charity toward the poor had always been very great; but it was so much redoubled at the end of his life that I could give him no greater pleasure than to talk with him about it. For four years he had been exhorting me with great earnestness to devote myself to the service of the poor, and to bring my children to it. And when I told him I feared that this might distract me from the care of my family, he told me that this was only a want of good will, and that, as there are various degrees in this virtue, one may well practise it in such a way that it does no harm to domestic affairs. He said that it was the general vocation of Christians, and that no particular sign was needed to know whether one was called to it, because it was certain; that it is on this that Jesus Christ will judge the world; and that when one considered that the mere omission of this virtue is a cause of damnation, this thought alone was enough to bring us to strip ourselves of everything, if we had faith. He told us further that visiting the poor is extremely profitable, in that, seeing continually the miseries with which they are overwhelmed, and that even in the extremity of their illnesses they lacked the most necessary things, one would have to be very hard after that not to deprive oneself willingly of useless comforts and superfluous finery.

All these talks stirred us up and sometimes led us to make proposals for finding means toward general regulations that would provide for every need; but he did not approve of this, and said that we were not called to the general, but to the particular; and that he believed the way most pleasing to God was to serve the poor poorly, that is to say, each according to his means, without filling one's mind with those grand designs that smack of that excellence whose pursuit he condemned in all things. Not that he disapproved of the founding of general hospitals; on the contrary, he had a great love for them, as he clearly showed by his will; but he said that these great undertakings were reserved for certain persons whom God destined for them and whom He guided almost visibly, but that they were not the general vocation of everyone, as the daily and personal relief of the poor is.

These are some of the instructions he gave us to lead us to the practice of this virtue, which held so great a place in his heart; it is a small sample that shows us the greatness of his charity. His purity was no less; and he had so great a reverence for this virtue that he was continually on guard to keep it from being wounded, either in himself or in others; and it is not to be believed how strict he was on this point. I was even afraid on account of it, for he found fault with things I said which I thought quite innocent, and afterwards showed me their faults, which I should never have recognised without his counsel. If I sometimes said that I had seen a beautiful woman, he grew vexed and told me that one should never say such a thing before lackeys or young people, because I did not know what thoughts I might arouse in them by it. Nor could he bear the caresses I received from my children, and he told me that they should be broken of the habit, that it could only do them harm, and that one could show them tenderness in a thousand other ways. Such were the instructions he gave me on this subject, and such was his vigilance for the preservation of purity in himself and in others.

An incident befell him about three months before his death which was a very striking proof of this, and which shows at the same time the greatness of his charity. As he was returning one day from Mass at Saint-Sulpice, a young girl of about fifteen, very beautiful, came up to him and asked for alms. He was moved to see this person exposed to so evident a danger; he asked her who she was and what obliged her thus to beg; and having learned that she was from the country, that her father was dead, and that her mother, having fallen ill, had been carried to the Hôtel-Dieu that very day, he believed that God had sent her to him the moment she was in need; so that within the hour he took her to the seminary, where he placed her in the hands of a good priest, to whom he gave money, asking him to take care of her and to find her a situation where, because of her youth, she might receive guidance and where her person would be safe. And to relieve him in this charge, he told him that he would send him a woman the next day to buy her clothes and everything she needed to fit her to serve a mistress. The next day he sent him a woman, who worked so well with this good priest that, after having her clothed, they placed her in a good situation. And when this clergyman asked the woman the name of the one who was doing this charity, she told him that she had no leave to tell it, but that she would come to see him from time to time to provide for the girl's needs; and he begged her to obtain his permission to tell him his name: “I promise you that I will never speak of it during his lifetime; but if God should allow him to die before me, it would be a comfort to me to make this deed known; for I find it so beautiful that I cannot bear for it to remain forgotten.” Thus from this single incident that good clergyman, without knowing him, judged how much charity he had and how much love for purity. He had an extreme tenderness for us; but this affection did not go as far as attachment. He gave a very striking proof of it at the death of my sister, which preceded his own by ten months. fields.title: His Last Illness and Death
fields.body_html:
It began with a strange distaste for food which came upon him two months before his death. His physician advised him to abstain from solid food and to take purges, and while he was in this state he performed a very remarkable act of charity. He had in his house a good man with his wife and his whole household, to whom he had given a room and whom he supplied with firewood, all of it out of charity, for he drew no other service from them than not being alone in his house. This good man had a son who, having fallen ill of smallpox at that time, gave my brother, who needed my help, cause to fear that I might be afraid to come to his house on account of my children. This obliged him to think of separating himself from the sick boy; but, as he feared the child would be in danger if he were carried out of the house in that condition, he chose rather to leave it himself, although he was already very ill, saying: “There is less danger for me in this change of lodging; that is why it must be I who leave.” So he left his house on the 29th of June to come to us, and he never returned to it; for three days later he began to be seized with a very violent colic which robbed him entirely of sleep. But as he had great strength of mind and great courage, he bore his pains with admirable patience. He nonetheless got up every day and took his remedies himself, refusing to let anyone render him the least service. The physicians who attended him saw that his pains were considerable; but because his pulse was very good, without any irregularity or sign of fever, they assured us that there was no danger at all, even using these words: “There is not the slightest shadow of danger.” Notwithstanding this, seeing that the continuance of his pains and his long sleepless nights were weakening him, on the very fourth day of his colic, and even before he had taken to his bed, he sent for the curé and made his confession. This caused a stir among his friends and brought several of them to see him, quite alarmed. The physicians themselves were so surprised that they could not help showing it, saying that it was a mark of apprehension they had not expected from him. My brother, seeing the disturbance this had caused, was vexed by it and said to me: “I should have liked to receive communion; but since I see that people are surprised at my confession, I fear they would be still more so; that is why it is better to put it off.” The curé being of the same opinion, he did not receive communion. Meanwhile his illness continued; and as the curé came to see him from time to time, he never let one of these occasions pass without confessing, and said nothing of it for fear of alarming people, because the physicians still maintained that there was no danger in his illness; and in fact his pains did abate somewhat, so that he sometimes got up in his room. They never left him entirely, however, and at times they even returned; he was also growing very thin, which did not much alarm the physicians. But whatever they might say, he always said that he was in danger, and never failed to confess each time the curé came to see him. During that time he even made his will, in which the poor were not forgotten, and he had to restrain himself from giving them more, for he told me that if M. Périer had been in Paris and had consented to it, he would have disposed of all his property in favour of the poor. In short, he had nothing in his mind and heart but the poor, and he would sometimes say to me: “How is it that I have never done anything for the poor, though I have always had so great a love for them?” I said to him: “It is because you have never had wealth enough to give them great help.” And he answered me: “Since I had no wealth to give them, I ought to have given them my time and my labour; that is where I have failed. And if the physicians are right, and if God allows me to rise from this illness, I am resolved to have no other employment and no other occupation for the rest of my life than the service of the poor.” These are the sentiments in which God took him.

To this ardent charity he joined, during his illness, a patience so admirable that he edified and astonished everyone around him. To those who showed distress at seeing the state he was in, he said that for his part he felt none, and that he was even afraid of getting well; and when he was asked the reason, he said: “It is because I know the dangers of health and the advantages of sickness.” At the height of his pains, too, when people grieved to see him suffer them, he would say: “Do not pity me; sickness is the natural state of Christians, because in it one is as one ought always to be: in the suffering of ills, in the privation of all goods and of all the pleasures of the senses, free from all the passions that work upon us throughout the whole course of life, without ambition, without avarice, in continual expectation of death. Is it not thus that Christians ought to spend their lives? And is it not a great happiness when one finds oneself by necessity in the state in which one is bound to be, and has nothing else to do but submit humbly and peaceably? That is why I ask for nothing else but to pray God to grant me this grace.” Such was the spirit in which he endured all his ills.

He greatly desired to receive communion; but the physicians opposed it, saying that he could not do so fasting unless it were done at night, which they did not think fitting without necessity, and that to receive communion as viaticum one must be in danger of death; and since that was not his case, they could not advise it. This resistance vexed him, but he was forced to yield to it. Meanwhile, as his colic still continued, he was ordered to drink the waters, which did in fact relieve him greatly. But on the sixth day of drinking them, which was the fourteenth of August, he felt a great dizziness with a severe pain in the head; and although the physicians were not surprised at this, and assured us that it was only the vapour of the waters, he nonetheless made his confession, and begged with incredible urgency that he be given communion, and that in God's name some means be found to remedy all the difficulties that had been put to him until then. He pressed so hard for it that a person who happened to be present reproached him with being restless, and told him that he ought to yield to the judgement of his friends; that he was better, and had almost no colic left; and that, since nothing remained but a vapour from the waters, it was not right for him to have the Blessed Sacrament brought to him; that it was better to wait and perform this act in church. He replied: “People do not feel my illness, and they will be deceived in it; my headache has something very extraordinary about it.” Nevertheless, seeing so great an opposition to his desire, he dared not speak of it any more; but he said: “Since they will not grant me this grace, I should like to make up for it by some good work, and, not being able to communicate in the Head, I should like to communicate in His members. To that end I have thought of having here a poor sick man, to whom the same services may be rendered as to me; let a nurse be engaged for him expressly, and in short let there be no difference between him and me, so that I may have the consolation of knowing that there is one poor man as well cared for as I am, in the shame I feel at seeing myself in the great abundance of all things in which I find myself. For when I think that, at the very time I am so well provided for, there are countless poor people who are sicker than I am and who lack the most necessary things, it gives me a pain I cannot bear; and so I beg you to ask the curé for a sick man for the purpose I have in mind.”

I sent to the curé that very hour, and he sent word that there was none in a condition to be moved; but that, as soon as my brother was cured, he would give him a means of exercising charity by taking charge of an old man whom he would care for the rest of his life: for the curé did not then doubt that he would recover.

When he saw that he could not have a poor man in the house with him, he begged me, then, to do him the kindness of having him carried to the Incurables, because he had a great desire to die in the company of the poor. I told him that the physicians did not think it advisable to move him in the state he was in, which vexed him greatly; he made me promise that if he had a little respite I would give him this satisfaction.

Meanwhile, as the pain in his head increased, he bore it as he bore all his other ills, that is, without complaining; and once, at the height of his pain, on the seventeenth of August, he asked me to call a consultation of physicians; but at the same moment he was seized with a scruple and said to me: “I fear there is too much seeking after my own comfort in this request.” I nonetheless had it held; and the physicians ordered him to drink whey, still assuring him that there was no danger, and that it was only migraine mixed with the vapour of the waters. Yet whatever they might say, he never believed them, and he asked me to have a priest spend the night beside him; and I myself found him so ill that, without saying anything, I gave orders for candles to be brought and everything needed for him to receive communion the next morning.

The preparations were not in vain, but they served sooner than we had thought: for about midnight he was seized with a convulsion so violent that, when it had passed, we thought he was dead; and we had, along with all the rest, the extreme grief of seeing him die without the Blessed Sacrament, after he had asked for it so often and so urgently. But God, who willed to reward so fervent and so just a desire, suspended this convulsion as though by a miracle, and restored his judgement entirely, as in perfect health; so that the curé, entering his room with the Blessed Sacrament, cried out to him: “Here is He whom you have so greatly desired.” These words roused him fully; and as the curé came near to give him communion, he made an effort and raised himself halfway up unaided, in order to receive it with greater reverence; and when the curé questioned him, according to custom, on the principal mysteries of the faith, he answered distinctly: “Yes, monsieur, I believe all that with all my heart.” He then received the holy viaticum and extreme unction with such tender feeling that he shed tears. He made all the responses and thanked the curé; and when the curé blessed him with the holy ciborium, he said: “May God never forsake me!” These were as it were his last words; for after he had made his thanksgiving, a moment later his convulsions seized him again, and they never left him again nor allowed him a single instant of clear mind. They lasted until his death, which came twenty-four hours later, on the nineteenth of August 1662, at one o'clock in the morning, at the age of thirty-nine years and two months.
